title: How Much Water Does Rice Need? Ratios by Rice Type and Cooking Method

seo.title: How Much Water for Rice: Ratios by Type
seo.meta_description: The ratio depends on rice and method. Utah State guides use about 1:1.75 for white long-grain, 1:1.5 for white medium/short, 1:2 for brown basmati, and 1:2.25 for brown long-grain.
seo.search_intent: Learn how much water to use per cup of rice by variety and method and understand why one universal ratio does not work for every rice.

excerpt: There is no universal rice-to-water ratio. For stovetop absorption cooking, Utah State uses about 1 cup white long-grain rice to 1¾ cups water, white medium/short to 1½, brown basmati to 2, and brown long-grain to 2¼. Method, lid fit, and evaporation change the result too.
content_html:
There is no single water ratio that works for every type of rice. For covered stovetop absorption cooking, Utah State University Extension uses roughly 1 cup white long-grain rice to 1¾ cups water, 1 cup white medium or short grain to 1½ cups, and 1 cup brown long-grain rice to 2¼ cups.

The difference comes from variety, processing, grain structure, cooking time, and how much water evaporates before the rice finishes. That is why the familiar “two cups water to one cup rice” rule can work for some rice and leave other types too soft or too dry.

White long-grain: about 1¾ cups water per cup rice

Utah State’s guide uses 1¾ cups of water for one cup of white long-grain rice with an approximate 18–20 minute low-heat cooking time after the pot reaches a boil.

This works for a covered absorption method where liquid is taken up by the grain while some slowly evaporates. A loose lid or very wide pan can lose more water and may require adjustment.

White medium or short grain: less water in the same guide

For white medium- or short-grain rice, Utah State recommends 1½ cups water per cup of rice. These grains release more starch and are often used when a moister or stickier texture is desirable.

Do not transfer this ratio directly to risotto, paella, or boil-and-drain methods. Those techniques may add liquid gradually, intentionally evaporate more, or use excess water that is drained at the end.

Brown rice usually needs more water and much more time

The same table uses 2 cups water per cup of brown basmati or brown jasmine and 2¼ cups for brown long-grain rice. Cooking times approach 40–45 minutes because the bran layer slows hydration.

If brown rice remains firm after absorbing all the liquid, add a small amount of hot water and continue covered. There is no need to flood the pot and start over.

Black, red, and parboiled rice need their own references

Utah State places black rice around 1¾–2 cups water per cup rice, red rice anywhere from 2–3 depending on the variety, and parboiled rice near 2. This variation shows why a universal rule does not describe the entire category.

For specialty rice, package directions are particularly useful because cultivars and processing methods can change absorption and timing.

Cooking method can matter as much as rice type

In absorption cooking, the measured water has to end up inside the grains or evaporated, so the starting ratio is critical. In the excess-water method, rice cooks more like pasta in a large volume and is drained when tender; the precise initial ratio matters far less.

A rice cooker also controls evaporation differently from an uncovered saucepan. Copying one appliance’s ratio into another method can therefore change texture.

Lid fit and pan diameter change water loss

A tight lid keeps more steam in the pot. A very wide pan has more evaporative surface than a narrow one. Repeatedly lifting the lid to check the rice releases steam and can change the balance.

After cooking, Utah State recommends keeping rice covered for another 5–10 minutes. Resting allows steam and moisture to redistribute and helps the grain surface settle before fluffing.

Altitude changes timing as well

At higher altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, so Utah State notes that cooking may need to be longer. If rice remains firm after the water is gone, a little additional hot liquid and more covered time are usually better than simply turning the heat much higher.

The practical rule: start with a ratio appropriate for your rice: white long-grain about 1:1.75, white medium/short about 1:1.5, and brown rice around 1:2–2.25. Keep the lid on, use low heat and a resting period, then adjust small amounts on the next batch for your exact pan and rice.

The practical answer depends on method and context. One number can work well in one kitchen and poorly in another because of differences in equipment, temperature, portion size, or food. Use the first batch as calibration and change only one variable at a time to build your own repeatable reference.

faq.question: How much water for one cup of white long-grain rice?
faq.answer: Utah State suggests about 1¾ cups water for one cup rice in a covered absorption method.

faq.question: Is rice always cooked with two parts water to one part rice?
faq.answer: No. The ratio changes with variety, processing, and cooking method.

faq.question: What if the rice is still hard and the water is gone?
faq.answer: Add a small amount of hot water, cover, and cook a few minutes longer over low heat.
